title: Thomas Sunday
hook: the Sunday after Easter remembers Thomas; Catholics also keep Divine Mercy Sunday

segments.voice: Yesterday, Easter Monday, and two friends on the road who didn't know who was walking with them. Your line was walk to emmaus. Who did you walk with? Day one thousand thirty-eight.

Thomas was out when it happened. His friends find him and tell him they've seen Jesus alive, and he answers them plainly. In the King James Bible: "Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe." He isn't rude about it. He just says what it would take. Hands. Nails. Side. Nothing secondhand. For eight days, the story leaves him there, the one in the room who can't say what everyone else is saying. In the Orthodox calendar, the Sunday after Easter is named for him. Today, Thomas Sunday.

John tells it like this: "after eight days again his disciples were within, and Thomas with them." Doors shut. Jesus stands among them and says, "Peace be unto you." Then he turns straight to Thomas and offers him exactly what he asked for: "Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing." Notice two things. First, Jesus doesn't refuse the request. He answers it, almost word for word. Thomas named his terms, and the risen Jesus meets them. Second, John never says Thomas actually touched him. Some paintings show his finger in the wound, but the text goes straight to what he says: "My Lord and my God." The one who doubted out loud is the one who says it, to Jesus, face to face. Then comes a line meant for everyone who wasn't in that room: "blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed." And it's worth knowing who Thomas was before this. Earlier in John, when Jesus decides to go back toward danger, it's Thomas who says to the others, "Let us also go, that we may die with him." The nickname doubting Thomas isn't in the Bible. Some readers would rather call him honest Thomas, or brave Thomas. Churches keep this Sunday in different ways. In the Orthodox calendar it's called Thomas Sunday. Catholics also keep it as Divine Mercy Sunday, a day centered on God's mercy, and some readers hear the two fitting together: a wounded Christ, offering peace, to a friend who couldn't yet believe.

Here's the practice: bring one honest question into the quiet. Settle, and breathe. Let one doubt come up, about faith, or about anything you're asked to trust. Don't argue it down. Don't polish it. Say it to yourself the way Thomas did, plainly, with your terms: this is what it would take. If you pray, you can bring that doubt to God just as it is, the way Thomas said his out loud. If you don't, simply hold the question with a bit of respect, as a sign you're paying attention. The bell holds the time.
Thomas Sunday. The Sunday after Easter, remembering the disciple who said what it would take to believe, and then said, my Lord and my God.
Your line: my lord and my god. Today, when someone asks a hard question, yours or theirs, answer it, or let it stand, instead of shushing it. Day one thousand thirty-eight.

howItsDone: In a number of churches, John 20's story of Thomas is read on the Sunday after Easter; the Orthodox call it Thomas Sunday, and Catholics also keep it as Divine Mercy Sunday.
